subject: pathology
title: Warm and Cold Autoimmune Haemolysis, PNH, Microangiopathy, and Newborn Haemolytic Disease

steps.tx: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia coats red cells with IgG at body temperature, splenic macrophages strip membrane into spherocytes, and the direct antiglobulin test glows positive for IgG with or without complement. Steroids are first line therapy for **warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia**. This point is tested repeatedly because it changes everyday bedside decisions.
steps.say: Warm IgG, spherocytes, positive Coombs: steroids first for warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

vis.caption: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia pathophysiology with IgG coating and splenic destruction.

steps.tx: Cold agglutinin disease uses IgM that binds red cells in cool peripheries, fixes complement, then detaches centrally leaving C3d coated cells for hepatic destruction and acrocyanosis in winter. Thermal amplitude decides symptoms in **cold agglutinin disease**, often clonal in older adults. Examiners return to it because it separates careful clinicians from guesswork.
steps.say: Cold IgM agglutinates in fingers and fixes complement; warmth avoidance and rituximab anchor treatment.

steps.tx: The direct Coombs test washes patient red cells and adds antihuman globulin to reveal antibody or complement already bound in vivo, while the indirect test hunts antibody in serum against reagent cells. The direct antiglobulin test, DAT, is the **direct Coombs test**.
steps.say: Direct Coombs finds antibody already on the patient's cells; indirect finds it waiting in serum.

steps.tx: Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria follows childhood viral illness with a biphasic Donath-Landsteiner IgG that binds in cold and haemolyses intravascularly on rewarming, dark urine included. The biphasic haemolysin is the **Donath-Landsteiner antibody**. Bedside recognition of this pattern saves time, blood, and unnecessary investigation.
steps.say: Donath-Landsteiner antibody binds cold and bursts cells warm: post-viral dark urine in a child.

nodes.label: Cold exposure: IgG binds P antigen

steps.tx: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria clones lose the GPI anchor for CD55 and CD59, leaving red cells naked before complement, causing night haemoglobinuria, thrombosis in odd veins, and marrow failure. Flow cytometry for missing anchors diagnoses **paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)**. Students should anchor this fact before moving to rarer causes and exceptions.
steps.say: Missing CD55 and CD59 anchors define PNH; eculizumab blocks the complement that destroys its cells.

vis.caption: PNH haemolysis from lost complement regulators and eculizumab blockade of terminal complement.

steps.tx: CD55 decays complement convertases and CD59 blocks the membrane attack complex, so their shared GPI anchor failure explains why complement, not antibody, is the executioner in PNH. The anchor is **glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)**, lost through PIGA mutation in the clone. In practice this distinction decides the next test, treatment, or referral made.
steps.say: One PIGA mutation removes the GPI anchor, both CD55 and CD59 vanish, and complement attacks unopposed.

steps.tx: Microangiopathic haemolysis shears red cells on fibrin strands in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, haemolytic uraemic syndrome, DIC, and malignant hypertension, littering film with schistocytes while platelets fall. The sheared fragment is the **schistocyte**, and its presence is a haematological emergency flag. That is why this detail earns its place in every examination and ward round.
steps.say: Schistocytes plus low platelets is an emergency: think TTP first and do not wait for the full pentad.

steps.tx: Haemolytic disease of the newborn pits maternal IgG, classically anti-D, against fetal red cells, causing anaemia, hydrops, and kernicterus risk, prevented by antenatal and postnatal anti-D prophylaxis. The prevented catastrophe is **haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn**. Remembering it prevents the commonest errors made with this presentation entirely.
steps.say: Anti-D prophylaxis turned a killing disease rare; maternal IgG crossing the placenta remains its mechanism.
